title: AI Firms Are Reportedly Buying Nvidia RTX 5090 GPUs in Bulk for Server Use
content:
Sunday, September 13th 2026
	
									
	
	
	
AI Firms Are Reportedly Buying NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPUs in Bulk for Server Use
New photos shared by HKEPC allegedly show pallets of brand-new, boxed GeForce RTX 5090 cards being unpacked at AI server assembly sites. Notably, these firms are not using the RTX PRO 6000 or dedicated data center accelerators NVIDIA actually markets for that work. The cards in question are standard retail RTX 5090s, the same cards gamers have struggled to find at anywhere close to MSRP, being pulled straight from their packaging and slotted into multi-GPU AI rigs. It must be mentioned that some elements of these photos appear to be altered, or at least edited with AI, so take these with a bit of caution.
Despite that, the current situation is not entirely new. During the crypto boom, miners bought up GeForce cards in bulk while gamers got squeezed out, and NVIDIA eventually responded with Lite Hash Rate models that throttled mining performance without touching gaming specs. That restriction got fully bypassed within about a year. This time, the workload is AI instead of mining, but the outcome for gamers looks familiar. As a result, retail RTX 5090 pricing has reportedly climbed past $5,000 on some listings, more than double its $1,999 launch price. Industry analysts even warned about this possibility months ago, and we now have a good idea why the RTX 5090 is at the price it's at.Notably, the cards in these shared photos aren't even RTX 5090D or v2 variants, the China-specific SKUs NVIDIA already nerfed for AI workloads to comply with export rules. That means NVIDIA has already proven it knows how to limit a GeForce card's AI performance while keeping gaming performance intact, yet hasn't applied that same restriction to the standard RTX 5090 sold everywhere else. Given how central AI has become to NVIDIA's business, it seems unlikely the company will step in this time either.

report.summary: AI firms are reportedly buying retail RTX 5090 GPUs in bulk for server builds, pushing street prices past $5,000 and squeezing gamers, echoing the crypto-mining shortage.
report.background: The RTX 5090 is NVIDIA's consumer flagship, with 32 GB of GDDR7 and high memory bandwidth that makes it unexpectedly attractive for AI inference and fine-tuning when data-center GPUs are scarce or costly. Data-center accelerators like H100, B200 and RTX PRO 6000 remain allocation-constrained, and export controls have pushed Chinese buyers toward nerfed 5090D/v2 SKUs. The crypto boom offered a preview: miners bought GeForce cards in bulk, gamers faced shortages, and NVIDIA shipped Lite Hash Rate models that were bypassed within a year. This time the workload is AI. Reports and photos from HKEPC allegedly show pallets of boxed retail 5090s at AI server assembly sites, though some images may be AI-edited, so caution is warranted. Retail pricing has reportedly climbed past $5,000, more than double the $1,999 launch MSRP.
key_points: HKEPC shared photos allegedly showing pallets of brand-new, boxed retail RTX 5090 cards being unpacked at AI server assembly sites. These are standard consumer cards, not NVIDIA's RTX PRO 6000 or data-center accelerators. Some elements of the images appear AI-altered, so the report should be treated cautiously.

Retail RTX 5090 prices have reportedly exceeded $5,000, over double the $1,999 launch MSRP. Analysts warned months ago that AI demand could absorb consumer supply. The dynamic mirrors the crypto-mining era, when bulk GPU buying left gamers paying inflated prices for scarce cards.

NVIDIA already sells China-specific RTX 5090D and v2 variants with AI performance deliberately reduced for export compliance, proving it can segment AI and gaming workloads. It has not applied similar limits to the global RTX 5090, and given AI's centrality to its business, intervention seems unlikely.

The crypto boom's Lite Hash Rate response was fully bypassed within about a year and did little to protect gamers long-term. AI firms buying retail cards may similarly evade any future restrictions, since multi-GPU inference and fine-tuning care more about VRAM capacity and bandwidth than official product tiers.
report.impact: For the AI industry, cheap 32 GB Blackwell cards offer a low-cost path to local inference, fine-tuning, and small training clusters, blurring the line between consumer and data-center hardware. That can help startups and researchers bypass allocation queues, but it also strains NVIDIA's product segmentation and could cannibalize higher-margin enterprise sales. Developers gain access to powerful VRAM at retail, though they face non-ECC memory, poor server cooling, warranty issues, and volatile pricing; cloud GPUs remain a safer alternative. Regular users and gamers bear the clearest cost: scarce stock, inflated prices, and a sense that NVIDIA is prioritizing AI revenue over its traditional gaming audience.
report.tools: To follow up, watch NVIDIA's RTX PRO 6000, L40S and H100/H200 for official server use, plus AMD Instinct MI325X as an alternative. For local AI, try vLLM, llama.cpp, Ollama and ExLlamaV2 on high-VRAM consumer cards. Cloud options include RunPod, Lambda Labs and Vast.ai. Track GPU prices via NowInStock, Tom's Hardware's GPU price index, and r/LocalLLaMA discussions.
